newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end lackluster session higher.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end lackluster session higher.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended higher for the third straight session on Monday, as continued bullish sentiment pushed the market higher.
Trading activity was very light and the session was described as terribly boring in the absence of economic reports or other market moving news.
Plus, with a slew of data on tap Tuesday, players opted to sit on the sidelines -- especially with Treasuries at the top of recent ranges and with yields down to levels not seen since late February.
"We're a little overbought but no one wants to sell aggressively," said Kevin Sweeney, head trader at CoreStates Bank.

"The market is in good shape and is dramatically improved (over the past month)," he added. "But for us to mount additional gains, we will have to see more (economic) numbers that are juicy and positive for the market."
In late trading on Monday, the 30-year bond was at 99-5/32, up 15/32, with its yield down to 6.69 percent -- its lowest level since closing at 6.66 percent on February 25.
"Guys come in and buy, and no one challenges them, so prices go up," said Vincent Verterano, head trader at Nomura Securities International Inc.

Yet, the short end had some trouble holding onto its gains. The two-year note closed up 1/32 at 100-14/32 to yield 6.01 percent. For the second straight day, the issue's yield dipped to 5.99 percent but failed to hold that level.
"The short end is bumping up against a ceiling," said Sweeney.
He noted that much of the recent wave of buying has not been totally voluntary.

The market is seen keying most on the May consumer price index, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. Overall CPI is expected to have risen 0.2 percent in May, with CPI ex-food and energy also seen up 0.2 percent.

Traders said that as long as the CPI doe not rise more than 0.2 percent, the market has room to roam because further benign inflation data would continue the low inflation environment. And, it would be another reason for the Federal Reserve to leave rates steady.
"The market is becoming accustomed to the Fed-on-hold-for the foreseeable future view," Sweeney said.
"There's been some reluctant buying as people have been dragged in because they are not seeing dips," he said. "People are putting money to work with wailing and gnashing their teeth."
Others noted that with just about all of the market's short positions having been covered, it will take retail buying to push the market higher.
That, traders said, could come as early as Tuesday morning, when three major economic reports will be released. The data collectively are expected to be on the weak side.
Already, the market has factored out all odds of a rate hike in July and discounting one in August is not far behind, traders said.

Treasuries opened firmer on Monday and continued to grind higher throughout the day, partially on the hope that the Fed would do another coupon pass round and the reinvestment of the $30 billion cash management bill, maturing on Tuesday.

As of 1500 EDT, trading volume was $47.1 billion, nine percent below an average Monday in the second quarter, according to GovPX. Bill volume was 35 percent below average and coupon volume was 11 percent below normal.
Five-year notes rose 4/32 to 100-31/32 to yield 6.27 percent and the 10-year note was up 9/32 to 101-22/32 to yield 6.39 percent.
Three-month bill rates were unchanged at 4.84 percent, six-month rates were unchanged at 5.11 percent and year bill rates were down one basis point at 5.33 percent.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
